overview.body:
**Nuada** (*nuada*) — War, King of Tuatha · First King of the Tuatha Dé Danann — is the silver-handed king whose story turns on the body of the ruler: he lost his right arm winning Ireland from the Fir Bolg, lost his throne to the law that no blemished man may be king, and won both back through the craft of the physician-gods.[^1]

Old Irish *Nuadu* (later *Nuada*) bears the byname *Airgetlám*, 'Silver-hand', from the arm of silver the physician [[diancecht|Dian Cécht]] made him after the First Battle of Mag Tuired. The name itself belongs to one of the clearest pan-Celtic families: Welsh Nudd and Lludd Llaw Eraint ('Lludd of the Silver Hand') and the Gaulish Nodens of Lydney Park stand beside the Irish king, and scholars reconstruct a Common Celtic stem behind all three — though its meaning, 'cloud-maker' or 'catcher, fisher', remains honestly debated.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Nuada** — identical, letter for letter, to the attested medieval spelling. No form of the name is currently held as a domain: the plain ASCII *nuada.com* is registered to a third party outside the collection and is watched for release, so this temple stands without an owned address. Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: there is no diacritic or distinctive letter for ASCII to lose.[^3]

sources.citation: Lebor Gabála Érenn, ed. and trans. R. A. S. Macalister, 5 vols., Irish Texts Society 34, 35, 39, 41, 44 (London: Irish Texts Society, 1937–56), vol. 4 (Tuatha Dé Danann; First Battle of Mag Tuired; Airgetlám; Bres).
Mac Cana, Proinsias, Celtic Mythology, 3rd ed. (London: Chancellor Press, 1996), s.v. Nuadu, Nudd, Nodens.
Koch, John T. (ed.), Celtic Culture: A Historical Encyclopedia, 5 vols. (Santa Barbara: ABC-CLIO, 2006), s.v. Nuadu Airgetlám, Nodens, Lydney Park.

the-name.body:
The name is attested in Old Irish as **Nuadu** (Middle Irish and modern **Nuada**; modern Irish **Nuadha**), with the byname *Airgetlám* — *airget* 'silver' + *lám* 'hand, arm'.[^1] Its etymology is debated and this edition treats it as such: one proposal reads the name as 'cloud-maker', connecting it with Welsh *nudd* 'mist'; the other, argued by Tolkien for the Gaulish form, derives it from a root meaning 'to catch, acquire, make use of' — a 'catcher' or fisher-hunter, which would fit the hounds and fishermen of the Lydney temple imagery.[^2]

The cognate chain is the name's strongest evidence. Welsh **Nudd** and **Lludd Llaw Eraint** ('Lludd of the Silver Hand') translate the Irish byname word for word; Gaulish **Nodens** (also written Nodons, Nudens) is the dedicatory name of the temple at Lydney Park in Gloucestershire. Mac Cana and Koch reconstruct a Common Celtic *Noudont- / *Noudo- behind all three forms.[^1]

Because the attested spelling is plain ASCII, the letter-by-letter transformation is the identity map:

- **n** → **N** — Same, capitalized
- **u** → **u** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **d** → **d** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same

The name is classified Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the restoration preserves no diacritic and no distinctive letter, because the medieval scribes wrote none. The project holds no domain for this entry: *nuada.com* is registered outside the collection and is watched for release, and this temple claims no address.[^3]

sources.citation: Mac Cana, Proinsias, Celtic Mythology, 3rd ed. (Chancellor Press, 1996); Koch, John T. (ed.), Celtic Culture: A Historical Encyclopedia (ABC-CLIO, 2006), s.v. Nuadu.

Wheeler, R. E. M., and T. V. Wheeler, Report on the Excavation of the Prehistoric, Roman, and Post-Roman Site in Lydney Park, Gloucestershire (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1932), Appendix I: J. R. R. Tolkien, 'The Name "Nodens"'.
Jackson, Kenneth Hurlstone, The Oldest Irish Tradition: A Window on the Iron Age (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1964), on early Irish name-forms and kingship.

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the Old Irish form is **/ˈnuː.að.u/** — Old Irish Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **N-** — Broad alveolar nasal [n̪ˠ], unlenited, as in every Old Irish initial n
- **-uː-** — Long close back [uː], stressed on the first syllable as in all Old Irish words
- **-a-** — Open [a] across the syllable boundary
- **-ð-** — Lenited d, the voiced dental fricative [ð] of English *this*; medieval scribes wrote the lenition without marking it
- **-u** — Short final [u], the nominative ending of the earliest form Nuadu

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'NOO-ah-oo' — the first vowel long, the middle consonant softened toward 'th', the ending short. The everyday modern pronunciation 'NOO-uh-duh' is an anglicized convenience, not the medieval sound.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Old Irish** — Nuadu, later Nuada; byname Airgetlám, 'Silver-hand'
- **Middle Welsh** — Nudd; Lludd Llaw Eraint, 'Lludd of the Silver Hand'
- **Gaulish** — Nodens (Nodons, Nudens), as inscribed at Lydney Park[^2]
- **Modern Irish** — Nuadha, the living form

Nuada is Tier 2 because the attested form is already plain ASCII: there is nothing for the restoration to recover, and the temple is honest about that — the work here is scholarly, not orthographic.

sources.citation: Thurneysen, Rudolf, A Grammar of Old Irish, rev. ed., trans. D. A. Binchy and Osborn Bergin (Dublin: Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies, 1946), phonology.
Koch, John T. (ed.), Celtic Culture: A Historical Encyclopedia (ABC-CLIO, 2006), s.v. Nodens, Nuadu.

original-script.body:
The name is preserved in medieval Irish vellum manuscripts in the Insular Latin bookhand as **Nuadu / Nuada** — Old Irish, recorded in the recensions of the Lebor Gabála Érenn and in the battle texts of the Mythological Cycle, which survive in late-medieval and early-modern codices but preserve much older material.[^1] No Ogham inscription names him; the Insular manuscript form is the primary witness.

The rendering is straightforward because the scribes left nothing for modern editors to restore:

- The name is a single stem, *Nuadu*, with the nominative ending intact; the byname *Airgetlám* compounds *airget* 'silver' and *lám* 'hand, arm'.
- Old Irish orthography of the manuscript period does not mark vowel length or lenition with diacritics in this name, so the attested spelling is plain ASCII.
- In the Ogham letter-row the name would have been notched **ᚅᚒᚐᚇᚐ** (N-U-A-D-A) — a mechanical transliteration, not an attested carving; no stone yet found carries the theonym.[^2]
- The Unicode form Nuada is therefore identical to the ASCII input, and the temple says so rather than inventing marks the sources do not contain.

sources.citation: Lebor Gabála Érenn, ed. and trans. Macalister, Irish Texts Society (1937–56).
McManus, Damian, A Guide to Ogam, Maynooth Monographs 4 (Maynooth: An Sagart, 1991), on the Ogham alphabet.

domains.body:
**Nuada** rules where kingship, war, and healing meet: he is the king whose right to rule was settled by his body's wholeness, the war-leader of both battles of Mag Tuired, and the patient of the two greatest healings in the Irish corpus.[^1]

### Kingship

First king of the Tuatha Dé Danann in Ireland; the blemish law unseated him and his restoration confirmed the law's symmetry — it unseated the unjust Bres by the same standard.

### War

Victor of the First Battle of Mag Tuired against the Fir Bolg; lord of the sword from Findias that none escaped; fallen commander at the Second Battle, yielding the champion's seat to [[lugh|Lúg]] before the fighting.

### Healing

The recipient of Dian Cécht's silver arm and of Miach's greater healing, 'joint to joint and vein to vein' — the mythic proof-text for healing as a sovereign art.

### Justice (as Nodens)

At Lydney Park his Gaulish cognate heard the curse of Silvianus against a ring-thief: the god who withholds health until wrong is put right.[^2]

sources.citation: Lebor Gabála Érenn, ed. and trans. Macalister (1937–56); Cath Maige Tuired, ed. and trans. Elizabeth A. Gray, Irish Texts Society 52 (London: Irish Texts Society, 1982).
Wheeler and Wheeler, Lydney Park report (1932); the Silvianus curse tablet (RIB 306).

symbols.body:
Nuada's iconography is narrative and, uniquely among Irish gods, also archaeological — through his Gaulish cognate the name has a real temple inventory:[^1]

- **The silver arm** — Dian Cécht's masterpiece, made with Credne the brazier, moving in every joint: wholeness restored by craft, and the source of the byname Airgetlám
- **The sword from Findias** — one of the Four Treasures the Tuatha Dé Danann brought from the northern cities of the world; once drawn, no one escaped from it[^2]
- **Tara (Temair)** — the seat of the kingship of Ireland, where the blemish law was enforced and where Nuada yielded the champion's seat to Lugh
- **The physician's toolkit** — silver-work and flesh-work: the arm made by art and the arm regrown by healing, the two technologies of restoration
- **Dog and fisherman (as Nodens)** — the bronze hounds and sea imagery of the Lydney temple, where the name's oldest recoverable meaning — hunter, catcher, fisher — seems still to be speaking[^3]

sources.citation: Lebor Gabála Érenn, ed. and trans. Macalister (1937–56).
The Four Treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann (Do Fhalitus na Túatha Dé Danann), in the Lebor Gabála tradition, ed. Macalister.
Wheeler and Wheeler, Lydney Park report (1932), catalogue of finds.

mythology.body:
Nuada's mythology is a single continuous arc across two battles and one interregnum: the arm, the silver, the satire, the return, and the death. The [[dagda|Dagda]], [[ogma|Ogma]], and [[lugh|Lúg]] move through it as comrades; [[balor|Balor]] ends it.[^1]

### The First Battle of Mag Tuired (Lebor Gabála; Fraser's 'First Battle of Moytura')

The Tuatha Dé Danann, come to Ireland with Nuada seven years their king, demanded the country from the Fir Bolg. At Mag Tuired in Connacht the battle was joined, and Nuada fought Sreng, the Fir Bolg champion: Sreng struck off his right arm at the shoulder, yet the Tuatha Dé Danann carried the field, and the Fir Bolg king Eochaid mac Eirc was driven to his death seeking water. Ireland was won — by a king now unwhole.[^2]

### The Silver Hand, and the Hand of Flesh (Lebor Gabála)

The law held that no man with a blemish could be king of Ireland, so the sovereignty passed to Bres mac Elatha. Dian Cécht the physician, with Credne the brazier, made Nuada a full arm of silver that moved in every joint — hence Airgetlám. Then Dian Cécht's son Miach did the impossible thing: he laid the severed arm to the stump and healed it 'joint to joint and vein to vein' in thrice nine days. Dian Cécht, envious of the son who had outdone the father, struck Miach dead; from the grave grew three hundred and sixty-five herbs, one for every joint and sinew, which Miach's sister Airmed spread on her mantle in their order — and which Dian Cécht scattered, so that the complete art of healing perished with his jealousy.[^1]

### Bres and the First Satire in Ireland (Lebor Gabála; Cath Maige Tuired)

Bres ruled as his blood dictated: the champions of Ireland were put to carrying firewood and digging dykes, the knives were not greased at the feast, and the poet Cairbre mac Etaine, denied hospitality, made against Bres what the tradition counts the first satire in Ireland — and blisters rose on the king's face. The same blemish law that had unseated Nuada now unseated Bres; with his arm made flesh again, Nuada took back the kingship.[^1]

### The Second Battle and the King's Death (Cath Maige Tuired)

When the war with the Fomorians could no longer be delayed, a stranger came to Tara claiming every craft at once — 'I am a wright; a smith; a champion; a harper; a poet' — and the doorkeeper's rule was that no man without an art could enter. [[lugh|Lúg]] the Ildánach, the many-skilled, won his way to the chessboard, and Nuada, seeing in him the leader the war required, gave him his own seat. At the Second Battle of Mag Tuired, Nuada Airgetlám and [[macha|Macha]] his wife fell together at the hands of Balor of the Evil Eye; the Tuatha Dé Danann won the battle and buried their first king.[^3]

sources.citation: Lebor Gabála Érenn, ed. and trans. Macalister, vol. 4 (1937–56).
Fraser, J., 'The First Battle of Moytura', Ériu 8 (1916), 1–63.
Cath Maige Tuired, ed. and trans. Elizabeth A. Gray, Irish Texts Society 52 (1982), §§ on Lugh's arrival and the deaths of Nuada and Macha.

syncretism.body:
Nuada's cross-border identity is the strongest in the Celtic pantheon: a single name runs through three traditions with its silver hand intact. In Welsh he is **Nudd**, and in full form **Lludd Llaw Eraint** — 'Lludd of the Silver Hand', king of Britain in the tale *Lludd a Llefelys*, where he frees his realm from three plagues; the byname translates Irish Airgetlám word for word (*llaw* 'hand', *eraint* 'silver').[^1] In Gaulish he is **Nodens**, god of the temple at Lydney Park, where Roman dedicants equated him with Mars, and where the imagery of hounds and fishermen suggests the older meaning of the name still at work.

Roman Britain kept the name in stone. The Silvianus curse tablet calls on 'Lord Nodens' to deny the thief of a stolen ring his health until the ring reaches the god's temple — justice enforced through the body, the same logic as the Irish blemish law.[^2] Within the Irish corpus, closely related figures include [[lugh|Lúg]] (who inherits the war-leadership), [[diancecht|Dian Cécht]] (whose craft makes the king's name), and [[macha|Macha]] (the wife who falls beside him).

sources.citation: Lludd a Llefelys, in The Mabinogion, trans. Sioned Davies (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2007); Culhwch ac Olwen (Lludd Llaw Eraint).
Wheeler and Wheeler, Lydney Park report (1932); Silvianus curse tablet (RIB 306); Mac Cana, Celtic Mythology, 3rd ed. (1996), s.v. Nodens.

cultural-legacy.body:
Nuada's modern afterlife began in an excavation report. When the Wheelers published the Lydney Park dig in 1932, the appendix on the god's name was written by J. R. R. Tolkien, then Rawlinson and Bosworth Professor of Anglo-Saxon at Oxford — 'The Name "Nodens"' is a small classic of philology, and the Silchester ring associated with the Silvianus curse was shown to Tolkien decades later, fuelling the enduring (if unprovable) romance that the One Ring owes something to Nodens.[^1]

In Ireland the name never died: modern Irish Nuadha remains a given name, and Nuada's sword from Findias was borne on the old arms of St Patrick's College, Maynooth. Popular culture discovered him late but decisively — Guillermo del Toro's *Hellboy II: The Golden Army* (2008) made Prince Nuada Silverlance the most famous silver-handed figure in modern film — and the wider fantasy motif of the magical prosthetic hand descends, directly or not, from Airgetlám. In contemporary Celtic paganism Nuada is honoured as a god of rightful sovereignty, healing, and justice restored.[^2]

sources.citation: Wheeler and Wheeler, Lydney Park report (1932), Appendix I; Scull, Christina, and Wayne G. Hammond, The J. R. R. Tolkien Companion and Guide (London: HarperCollins, 2006), s.v. Nodens.
Koch, John T. (ed.), Celtic Culture: A Historical Encyclopedia (ABC-CLIO, 2006), s.v. Nuadu Airgetlám (reception).

archaeology.body:
In Ireland, Nuada is a figure of texts: no inscription, cult site, or votive deposit names him, and his evidence is the manuscript record of the Mythological Cycle.[^1] His Gaulish cognate, however, has one of the finest excavated sanctuaries in Roman Britain. The temple of Nodens at Lydney Park, Gloucestershire, set above the Severn estuary, was built in the later third century CE and rebuilt in the fourth; the Wheelers' excavations of 1928–29 uncovered its mosaic floors, guest-house and baths, and a rich votive assemblage: inscribed slabs reading DEVO NODENTI and D M NODONTI ('to the god Mars Nodens'), bronze dogs — the healer's animal — a relief of fishermen, and offerings of pins, bracelets, and coins.[^2]

The site's most haunting find is the curse tablet of Silvianus, who had lost a gold ring and dedicated half its value to Nodens on condition that the god deny health to the thief, 'among those who bear the name Senicianus', until the ring was brought to the temple. A gold ring inscribed SENICIANE VIVAS IN DEO ('Senicianus, may you live in God') was found at Silchester a century earlier, and the two are now displayed together as plausibly the very ring of the curse.[^3] On the Irish side the material witnesses are the codices: the Second Battle of Mag Tuired survives complete only in the sixteenth-century British Library Harley MS 5280, and the First Battle in a single late vellum copy edited by Fraser.

sources.citation: Koch, John T. (ed.), Celtic Culture: A Historical Encyclopedia (ABC-CLIO, 2006), s.v. Lydney Park, Nodens.
Wheeler, R. E. M., and T. V. Wheeler, Report on the Excavation of the Prehistoric, Roman, and Post-Roman Site in Lydney Park, Gloucestershire (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1932).
The Silvianus curse tablet, Roman Inscriptions of Britain 306; the Silchester ring, RIB 306 companion find (The Vyne, National Trust).

meditation.body:
Nuada is the king who had to be rebuilt. The myth does not soften the law that unmakes him — a blemished man cannot be king, and the rule is applied as firmly to the oppressive Bres as to the wounded hero — but it answers the law with the whole craft of the divine physicians: first silver, then flesh. Between the two arms lies the cycle's deepest thought, that a made thing can carry a man back to himself but cannot carry him all the way; Miach's healing is greater than Dian Cécht's, and it costs Miach his life.[^1]

What remains is a sovereignty defined by fitness rather than possession. Nuada surrenders the throne without rebellion, serves his people maimed, takes the kingship back without vengeance, and at the end surrenders his own seat to the young god whose skills the war needs. The first king of the Tuatha Dé Danann is, at every crisis, the one who lets go — of the throne, of the silver, of the seat of honour. The myth measures kingship by what a ruler is willing to give up for the thing he rules.

sources.citation: Lebor Gabála Érenn, ed. and trans. Macalister (1937–56); Cath Maige Tuired, ed. and trans. Gray (1982).

irish-cycles.body:
Nuada belongs to the Mythological Cycle, the stratum of Irish literature that recounts the settlements of Ireland and the deeds of the Tuatha Dé Danann. The Lebor Gabála Érenn ('Book of the Taking of Ireland') gives him his full biography: seven years king before the landing, the First Battle of Mag Tuired against the Fir Bolg, the silver arm and the kingship of Bres, and the restoration.[^1]

The cycle's two battle texts frame his reign. The First Battle of Mag Tuired — preserved in a single late vellum copy and edited by Fraser in Ériu 8 (1916) — is the story of the arm: Sreng's stroke, the physicians' work, and the strange courtesy of the treaty that ended the war. The Second Battle (Cath Maige Tuired, edited by Gray for the Irish Texts Society, 1982) is the story of the succession: Lugh's arrival at Tara, the yielding of the champion's seat, and the deaths of Nuada and Macha before Balor's eye.[^2] Later cycle material keeps his name alive chiefly through his sword, counted among the Four Treasures the Tuatha Dé Danann brought from the cities of Findias, Gorias, Murias, and Falias.

sources.citation: Lebor Gabála Érenn, ed. and trans. Macalister (1937–56); Fraser, 'The First Battle of Moytura', Ériu 8 (1916).
Cath Maige Tuired, ed. and trans. Gray (Irish Texts Society, 1982).

welsh-sources.body:
Welsh tradition preserves the name in two forms. **Nudd** stands in the genealogies and in Culhwch ac Olwen as father of Gwyn ap Nudd, king of the Tylwyth Teg — a shadow of the old god's sovereignty, transferred to the Otherworld.[^1] The fuller form is **Lludd Llaw Eraint**, 'Lludd of the Silver Hand': Culhwch ac Olwen names him among the heroes, and the independent tale Lludd a Llefelys makes him king of Britain, the ruler who with his brother Llefelys frees the island from three plagues — an invading people whose speech could be heard at any distance, a scream every May Eve that blighted the land, and a magician who stole the court's provisions.

The byname is the evidence that matters: *llaw* 'hand' + *eraint* 'silver' translates Irish *Airgetlám* exactly, and the philological consensus (Mac Cana, Koch) treats Irish Nuadu Airgetlám, Welsh Lludd Llaw Eraint, and Gaulish Nodens as one inheritance from Common Celtic *Noudont-, rather than as three borrowings.[^2] The Welsh king fights no battle for his hand — the silver is fossilized in the name long after the story that explained it was lost in Britain.

sources.citation: Culhwch ac Olwen, ed. Rachel Bromwich and D. Simon Evans (Cardiff: University of Wales Press, 1992).
Lludd a Llefelys, trans. Davies, The Mabinogion (Oxford, 2007); Mac Cana, Celtic Mythology, 3rd ed. (1996); Koch (ed.), Celtic Culture (2006), s.v. Lludd.

inscriptions.body:
No Ogham stone names Nuadu, and no Irish inscription of any kind preserves the theonym; the name's epigraphic record belongs entirely to its Gaulish cognate in Roman Britain.[^1] At Lydney Park the dedicatory slabs read DEVO NODENTI ('to the god Nodens') and D M NODONTI ('to the god Mars Nodens'), with the spelling varying across Nodens, Nodons, and Nudens — the variation itself a datum for the name's Common Celtic stem. The Silvianus tablet, a lead curse inscribed in good Roman cursive, asks the god to withhold the thief's health 'until he brings it to the temple of Nodens'.

The Ogham letter-row gives the Irish name a hypothetical epigraphy: notched on the edge of a stone, Nuada would run **ᚅᚒᚐᚇᚐ** — N-U-A-D-A, vowels on the centre-line, consonants across it. This is a mechanical transliteration for display, clearly labelled as such; no attested carving exists, and this edition claims none.[^2]

sources.citation: Wheeler and Wheeler, Lydney Park report (1932), inscriptions; Roman Inscriptions of Britain 306 (Silvianus tablet).
McManus, Damian, A Guide to Ogam (An Sagart, 1991).
